newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China, HK central banks to continue to cooperate.
newsitem.headline: China, HK central banks to continue to cooperate.

text.p: China will continue to cooperate with Hong Kong's de facto central bank to assure financial stability, Chen Yuan, deputy governor of the Peoples' Bank of China, said on Friday.

"We will continue to cooperate with the Hong Kong Monetary Authority because we are mutually dependent on each other. That cooperation will last for many, many years," Chen told Reuters Financial Television in an interview.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) carries out most of the functions of a central bank -- focusing on protecting the Hong Kong dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar and banking supervision. The Peoples' Bank of China is China's central bank.
"We hope that our joint efforts to keep the market stable and the currency stable will turn out to be very successful," Chen said.
Hong Kong reverts to China on July 1 after more than 150 year of British colonial rule.
Under the "one country, two systems" scenario to be enshrined in the Sino-British treaty governing the handover, China and Hong Kong will maintain separate monetary systems.
China and Hong Kong have signed a bilateral repurchase agreement pact to provide liquidity in times of currency instability.
But Chen said cooperation between the two monetary authorities was otherwise informal.

"We don't have any specific instrument to use between us other than the repo agreement, but we already keep very close contact," he said, adding "that is the most efficient way to cooperate on market disturbances."

For example, "recently the Hong Kong Monetary Authority had a market intervention to stabilise the exchange rate, and in the morning I got a phone call from (HKMA chief executive) Joseph Yam to apprise me of the situation," said Chen.
Chen said China had no plans in place to "bail out" Hong Kong markets in the event of a crisis, but stressed that he did not anticipate such a need.

The Bank of England stepped in to help stabilise the Hong Kong dollar in 1983 when jitters about the impending handover sent what was then a free floating currency tumbling, Hong Kong government officials have said.

Shortly afterwards, Hong Kong pegged its dollar to the U.S. unit, a peg that has held firm since. The following year, British and Chinese negotiators signed a treaty governing the handover which served to allay some uncertainty.
